chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Salih ibn al-Sindi, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Sa'id ibn Khuthaym, from Ma'mar ibn Khuthaym, who said:

Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said to me: 'What is your teknonym (kunyah)?' I said: 'I have not yet taken a teknonym, and I have no son, nor a wife, nor a slave girl.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'So what prevents you from that?' I said: 'A hadith reached us from Ali (peace be upon him).' He (peace be upon him) said: 'And what is it?' I said: 'It reached us from Ali (peace be upon him) that he said: The one who takes a teknonym and has no family, is Abu Ja'ar (Father of Dung).' So Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'Falsified! This is not from the hadith of Ali (peace be upon him). We (peace be upon him) take our children's teknonyms in their childhood, for fear of the nickname being attached to them.'

key_terms.أَبُو جَعْرٍ: Father of Dung (a derogatory term for one without children who uses a kunyah)
key_terms.النَّبَزِ: Nickname/Epithet (specifically the one that sticks if the expected child is not born)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on taking a teknonym (kunyah) if one has no children, according to Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him)?
ai.summary: This narration highlights the Shia scholarly distinction between authentic prophetic traditions and popular sayings, as Imam al-Baqir (AS) corrects Ma'mar's attribution of the 'Abu Ja'ar' phrase to Imam Ali (AS). It elucidates the practical wisdom behind the Ahl al-Bayt's practice of bestowing kunyahs on children early in life, serving as a preventative measure against the social stigma of being called 'Father of [Name]' if the child were to pass away or remain childless. This reflects a broader cultural and religious emphasis on preserving dignity and avoiding negative nicknames (nabaz) within the community.
